title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement
tools_required: 11mm or 13mm wrench (caliper bracket bolts — varies by year)

parts.name: Front brake pads (semi-metallic)
parts.part_number: Wagner ZD436 / Bosch BC436 / Akebono ACT436

parts.name: Brake cleaner (aerosol, non-chlorinated)
parts.vendor: CRC, Berryman, any auto parts store

citations.title: Cherokeeforum ZJ front brake replacement how-to
ZJ service info

summary: Front pads on the ZJ wear faster than the rears because the system is biased forward. Plan on 2 hours for both sides if it's your first time, 45 minutes once you've done it. Always replace pads in axle pairs — never one side.
description:
The ZJ uses a single-piston floating caliper up front, the same basic design as the XJ Cherokee and TJ Wrangler. Pads run $25–$45 a set; rotors $60–$100 a pair. Don't cheap out on rotors — the bottom-tier $25/rotor specials warp within a year in Phoenix heat or any city driving with frequent hard stops. Centric or Bosch coated rotors hold up.

Wagner ZD436, Bosch BC436, and Akebono ACT436 are all solid pad choices. Avoid the lowest-tier organic pads on a ZJ — the rotors are heavy enough that organic pads glaze quickly and start squealing within 5,000 miles. Semi-metallic is the right pad family for a 4,000-lb SUV that gets driven hard.

Before you start: pump the brake pedal a few times with the engine off to bleed pressure off the system, crack the master cylinder cap (helps the caliper piston retract without forcing fluid backward), and have a friend or some shop towels nearby because new-pad break-in always involves a couple of "interesting" stops.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts a quarter turn with the wheels on the ground, then jack and support the vehicle on jack stands. Never work under a vehicle held up only by a jack.
Remove the wheels. Inspect the caliper, slide pins, and dust boots for tears.
Crack the master cylinder cap (don't remove it fully — break the seal so fluid can move).
Push the caliper piston back into the bore. A large C-clamp against an old pad face works; a piston-retraction tool is faster.
Remove the two caliper guide bolts (13mm) and lift the caliper up and off. Hang it from the upper control arm with a bungee or coat hanger — never let it hang by the brake hose.
Slide the old pads out. Note the inboard pad has the wear-indicator clip on the inside.
Remove the two caliper bracket bolts (typically 11mm or 13mm hex, varies by year — some are an external E-Torx) and lift the bracket off.
Pull the old rotor straight off the hub. If it's stuck, give it a few sharp hits with a dead-blow hammer on the hat (not the friction surface).
Spray brake cleaner on the new rotor to remove the shipping oil. Slide the new rotor onto the hub.
Reinstall the caliper bracket. Torque the bracket bolts to 70 ft-lbs (verify in a 1993–1998 ZJ service manual for your year — some years spec higher).
Apply a thin film of silicone brake grease to the slide pin contact surfaces and the back of each pad where it touches the caliper.
Slide the new pads into the bracket. Lower the caliper over the pads.
Reinstall the two caliper guide bolts. Torque to 25–30 ft-lbs (per the FSM).
Reinstall the wheel. Torque lug nuts to 90 ft-lbs in a star pattern.

With the wheel back on, sit in the driver's seat and pump the brake pedal until it firms up — usually 3–5 pumps. **This step is mandatory.** Driving without pumping the pedal first means no brakes on the first stop.
Check the master cylinder level; top off with DOT 3.

Bed in the new pads: 6 to 8 firm stops from 30 mph to 5 mph, then 30 minutes of normal driving without sitting on the brake at a long stoplight (the pad material smears onto the rotor and creates the friction surface — sitting still while it's hot causes pad imprinting).
pros: Direct, well-documented job — no special tools required
One of the few brake jobs where DIY savings (~$200 over a shop) actually justify the time
A fresh front brake setup makes the ZJ feel like a different vehicle if the old pads were glazed
cons: Front pads wear roughly twice as fast as rears on the ZJ — plan on replacement every 30,000 to 50,000 miles in city driving
Cheap rotors will warp; the savings aren't worth it
Pumping the brake pedal before driving is non-negotiable — skip that step and the first stop is empty pedal to the floor

title: Coolant Flush — 4.0 and Magnum V8

parts.name: Mopar 5-year/100K extended-life antifreeze (OAT), 1 gal
parts.vendor: any auto parts store; Prestone Cor-Guard or equivalent is fine

citations.title: ZJ 4.0L coolant capacity (Haynes reference)
ZJ service info — cooling system

summary: The ZJ 4.0L cooling system holds about 12.7 quarts; the Magnum V8s hold about 14 quarts. Plan on flushing with distilled water twice, then refilling with a 50/50 mix of distilled water and extended-life antifreeze. Bleed the air through the bleed plug on the thermostat housing — skip that step and you'll overheat within 10 miles.
description:
A ZJ that's never had a coolant flush will run hot in Phoenix summer, especially with the AC on, and the heater core will weep onto the passenger floor mat before it finally gives up. The 4.0L straight-six and the Magnum V8s both share an aluminum radiator on a plastic tank — these tanks crack with age, and old acidic coolant accelerates the failure. Flushing every 50,000 miles is the cheapest insurance you can buy against a $250 radiator.

The original Mopar HOAT (red) coolant was good for 5 years or 100,000 miles. Modern Mopar extended-life OAT coolant is fully backward-compatible with the ZJ if the system is fully flushed first. Don't mix coolant chemistries — flush twice with distilled water until what comes out is clear, then refill with a single coolant type. Prestone Cor-Guard, Peak Long Life, and Mopar's current OAT spec all work.

The radiator drain is a plastic petcock on the passenger-side bottom of the radiator. Most are old, brittle, and snap off when you turn them with pliers. Have a $25 replacement petcock on hand before you start. The block drain is a 1/4" NPT plug on the driver's side of the block — pull that too if you want a full flush, but it's optional and clears most of the residual coolant.
steps: Run the engine until it's at full operating temperature, then shut down and let it cool for at least an hour. Hot coolant under pressure scalds — wait until the cap is cool to the touch.
Remove the radiator cap. Position a drain pan under the radiator petcock (passenger-side bottom).
Open the radiator petcock — twist counterclockwise, gently. If it cracks, replace with a new petcock before continuing.
Drain into the pan, then transfer to a 5-gallon bucket. Old coolant is hazardous waste — take it to an AutoZone or O'Reilly for free recycling.
Close the petcock, fill the radiator with distilled water. Run the engine with the heater on full hot for 10 minutes to circulate.
Shut down, let cool, drain. Repeat until what drains is clear — usually two cycles is enough.
Close the petcock for the last time. Refill with a 50/50 mix of distilled water and OAT coolant. The 4.0L needs about 6 quarts of each; the V8s need about 7 of each.
Open the bleed plug on the thermostat housing (top of engine, on the upper radiator hose inlet). Fill until coolant runs out of the bleed hole air-free. Close the bleed plug.
Top off the radiator. Leave the cap off, run the engine with the heater on full hot for 15 minutes, watching the temp gauge. Top off as the coolant level drops.
Install the cap, run it up to operating temp, drive a few miles. Re-check level the next day — overflow bottle should be between MIN and MAX cold.
pros: Cheap maintenance — $25 in supplies, no special tools
The single biggest predictor of long-term cooling system reliability
Catches a failing radiator or weeping water pump before they leave you stuck
cons: The plastic radiator petcock breaks more often than not on a ZJ that's never been serviced — have a spare on hand
Air pockets in the heater core will cause overheating even after a "good" flush — bleed the system properly or repeat the bleed procedure after the first drive
The old MEG (green) coolant must be fully flushed before refilling with OAT — mixing causes gelling and ruins the water pump

title: 42RE / 46RE Transmission Fluid Service
tools_required: drain pan (wide, low profile, 8+ qt capacity)
fluid pump or long-neck funnel (fill is through the dipstick tube)
skills_required: RTV bead control if reusing pan with no gasket
checking ATF level on a warm running transmission

parts.name: ATF+4 (5–6 quarts for filter+fluid drop, 10–12 for full flush)
parts.part_number: Mopar 05013457AA / Valvoline MaxLife ATF+4 / Castrol Transmax ATF+4

parts.name: Transmission filter and pan gasket kit (42RE)
Transmission filter and pan gasket kit (46RE V8)

citations.title: ExtremeTerrain — ZJ Service Information
JeepForum — 42RE fluid capacity discussion

summary: The 42RE (behind the 4.0L six) and the 46RE (behind the 5.2 and 5.9 Magnum V8s) are both updates to the old A500 / A518 series. They need ATF+4 — not Dexron, not Mercon, not "universal." A pan drop and filter swap takes 5 quarts and buys you 30,000 more miles of clutch life.
description:
ATF+4 is mandatory. The older ATF+3 (and the original ATF+) are superseded by ATF+4, and Mopar 05013457AA is the genuine fluid. Any ATF+4 that meets MS-9602 spec is acceptable — Valvoline MaxLife ATF+4 and Castrol Transmax both qualify. Do not run Dexron or Mercon. The frictional properties are wrong and you'll get shudder, late shifts, and eventual band damage.

A pan drop (the only practical home service — these transmissions have no drain plug) refreshes about 30% of the total fluid. Total capacity is 8.5–11 quarts dry; a service refill is 4.5–5 quarts. Plan to do a pan drop every 30,000 miles. If the fluid is burnt-smelling or dark brown instead of red, drop the pan, change the filter, and refill — then repeat the pan drop in 1,000 miles to swap more of the converter's fluid by dilution.

Service interval: 30,000 miles for normal driving. 15,000 for trail use or towing. If the previous owner never serviced it and you bought the ZJ used, do the service immediately — but if the fluid is already burnt-black, talk to a transmission shop before you do anything; a fresh-fluid shock can flush varnish loose and clog passages on a worn 42RE.
steps: Drive 15 minutes to warm the fluid. Warm ATF flows out cleanly and gives you the correct dipstick reading when you refill.
Park on a level surface and chock the front wheels. Set the parking brake firmly.
Jack the front of the vehicle and support it on jack stands. The transmission pan needs ground clearance for a drain pan underneath.

Slide the wide drain pan under the transmission pan. Loosen pan bolts (10mm or 13mm depending on year) from one corner first, working diagonally so the pan tilts and drains gradually rather than dumping all at once.
Once the flow slows, support the pan with one hand while removing the last few bolts. Lower it carefully — there's about a quart of fluid still in the pan.

Remove the filter (one or two bolts depending on year). The filter has an O-ring on the pickup — make sure it comes out with the filter and isn't stuck in the transmission. Losing the O-ring inside the trans is the most common mistake on this job.
Install the new filter with its new O-ring. Don't reuse the old O-ring even if it looks fine.
Clean the pan thoroughly. Wipe out the magnet — fine metal paste is normal, big chunks are bad news. Scrape off any old gasket material.

Install the new pan gasket. Most ATP and Hayden kits come with a reusable rubber gasket — no RTV needed if the kit includes a gasket. If reusing the pan with no gasket, run a 1/8" bead of high-temp RTV.
Reinstall the pan. Torque pan bolts to 13 ft-lbs in a criss-cross pattern. Don't over-torque — the pan flange warps if you crank past 18 ft-lbs.
Lower the vehicle. Add 4.5 quarts of ATF+4 through the dipstick tube using a long-neck funnel or pump.
Start the engine. With your foot on the brake, cycle through every gear position (P-R-N-D-3-2-1, hold each gear for 3 seconds). Return to Park.
Check the dipstick with the engine running and the trans at idle. Cold reading should be between the "Add" and the lower hash mark. Top off to the cold-fill line.
Drive 10 miles. Re-check the level at full operating temp with the engine running, in Park, on a level surface. Top off to the hot full mark.
Check the pan for leaks after the first drive and again 24 hours later.
pros: Cheap insurance for an aging transmission — clutches and bands last longer with clean fluid
Catches metal contamination on the pan magnet before it grinds through the planetary gears
A burnt-smelling drop tells you exactly what state the trans is in before you trail it
cons: Pan-drop service only refreshes ~30% of total fluid — for a true flush you need a shop machine
Aged ZJs with never-serviced fluid can react badly to fresh ATF — old varnish breaks loose and clogs valves
The 42RE/46RE doesn't have a drain plug, so the job is messier than a modern transmission
Over-torquing pan bolts warps the flange — this is the most common DIY mistake

title: Differential Fluid — Dana 30 / Chrysler 8.25 / Dana 44a
tools_required: 13mm socket (cover bolts on most ZJ axles)

parts.name: Gear oil 75W-90 (conventional or synthetic)
parts.part_number: Valvoline VV832 / Mobil 1 75W-90 / Royal Purple Max-Gear

citations.title: ExtremeTerrain — Grand Cherokee ZJ Fluid Capacities
Cherokee Forum — ZJ axle fluid service

summary: Front Dana 30 takes 1.25 quarts. Rear Chrysler 8.25 takes 2.1 quarts. Rear Dana 44a (5.9 Limited and V8 tow package) takes 2.6 quarts. All three want 75W-90 gear oil, and if your rear is Trac-Lok limited-slip you need 4 oz of friction modifier on top.
description:
This is one of the highest-payoff maintenance jobs on a used ZJ — most of them come with whatever fluid was in there when the previous owner stopped caring. Plan on 90 minutes for both axles your first time, half that on the second pass. The cover-off method (no drain plug on these axles) means you'll wipe out old fluid, scrape off the cover, and re-seal with RTV.

Figuring out which rear axle you have: pull the tag on a cover bolt. "8.25" is the Chrysler 8.25 (most 4.0L ZJs). "44" is the Dana 44a (most 5.2/5.9 Magnum ZJs and V8 trailer-tow packages). The Dana 30 is up front on every ZJ — no Dana 44 up front from the factory. The Dana 44a (the "a" is for aluminum center) is lighter than a full Dana 44 but uses the same ring and pinion, so service is the same.

Service interval: every 30,000 miles for street driving. Every 15,000 miles if you wheel, ford water above the diff, or tow regularly. Water intrusion turns gear oil milky — if you pull a cover and see chocolate milk, change it now and check for axle seal damage.
steps: Drive 10–15 minutes first so the gear oil is warm and flows out cleanly. Park on a level surface.
Loosen the lug nuts a quarter turn (wheels still on the ground), then jack and support the vehicle on jack stands. Both axles need to come off the ground so fluid drains evenly.
Position a wide, low drain pan under the diff cover.
Remove all but two of the top cover bolts (13mm on most ZJ axles). Leave one bolt at each upper corner snug — these hold the cover while you crack the seal.
Tap the cover gently with a rubber mallet to break the gasket. Fluid will start running out the bottom.
Once the flow slows, remove the two remaining bolts and pull the cover off. Catch the last cupful of fluid with a rag.
Scrape the old gasket or RTV off both the cover and the axle housing. A razor blade and brake cleaner finish the job. The mating surfaces need to be dry, clean, and oil-free.
Inspect the ring gear and the magnet inside the cover (if present). A small amount of fine metal paste on the magnet is normal. Big chunks of metal mean stop and call a shop.
Apply a 1/4" continuous bead of Ultra Black RTV around the cover, circling the bolt holes on the inside. Let it skin for 5 minutes per the Permatex instructions.
Bolt the cover back on. Torque cover bolts to 30 ft-lbs in a criss-cross pattern. Don't over-torque — stripped cover threads in cast aluminum (the 44a) are a real possibility.
Refill through the fill plug (3/8" square drive on the side of the axle housing). Fill until fluid barely weeps out of the fill hole.
Reinstall the fill plug. Torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Repeat for the second axle.
Drive the vehicle 10 miles, then re-check for leaks at the cover and fill plug. Re-torque cover bolts if needed after a heat cycle.
pros: Cheap insurance — a $30 fluid change extends ring-and-pinion life by 50,000+ miles
Catches problems early: water intrusion, broken teeth, axle seal failure
A clean cover gives you a baseline for future trail wheeling and water crossings
cons: The cover-off method is messier than a drain plug — the 8.25 and Dana 30 don't have one
Aluminum 44a cover threads strip if you over-torque — slow and careful with the torque wrench
Trac-Lok diffs absolutely need the friction modifier or you'll get chatter on tight turns

title: Oil Change — 4.0L and Magnum V8s
tools_required: jack and jack stands or ramps

parts.name: Engine oil — 10W-30 conventional or full synthetic

citations.title: Mopar oil filter compatibility (5281090AB / MO-090)
ZJ fluid capacities reference

summary: The ZJ takes 6 quarts of 10W-30 (4.0L) or 5 quarts (5.2/5.9L Magnum), and Mopar's MO-090 filter fits every engine option. Plan on 30 minutes if everything cooperates and the previous owner didn't overtighten the drain plug.
description:
The ZJ's 4.0L and Magnum V8s are old, low-stress engines that don't care which name brand of oil you run — they care that you run *some* clean oil and change it on time. Use a conventional 10W-30 for high-mileage rigs that already leak; jump to a full synthetic 5W-30 if you live in Phoenix or anywhere else where the engine bakes after shutdown. Skip the heavy 20W-50 unless you're in the middle of summer and watching pressure drop at idle on a tired motor.

Mopar's 5281090AB filter (the box also says MO-090) is the OEM unit and fits the 4.0L, 5.2L Magnum, and 5.9L Magnum — one part number across the whole engine lineup. Wix 51515, Purolator L25288, and Fram TG3614 are the common equivalents. Avoid the smallest Frams; a slightly oversized filter holds more oil and is more manageable to grip when it's hot.

Park on a level surface, run the engine for two minutes to warm and thin the oil, then shut it down. Pull the dipstick to break the vacuum (oil drains faster), set the pan, and crack the drain plug with a 13mm socket. The plug is a tapered design that doesn't need a crush washer, but if yours has been overtightened in the past and weeps, replace it with a Dorman 095-002 plug-and-gasket combo.
steps: Warm the engine for 2 minutes, then shut down. Set the parking brake and chock the rear wheels.
Raise the front of the vehicle on jack stands or drive onto ramps. Working flat on the ground is possible but miserable.
Position the drain pan, remove the dipstick, and loosen the drain plug with a 13mm socket. Let it drain for at least 5 minutes — longer if you have time.
Move the pan under the oil filter (passenger side, near the bottom of the block). Loosen with a filter wrench, then spin off by hand. Watch for the gasket — it should come off with the filter.
Wipe the filter mounting surface clean. Smear fresh oil on the new filter's gasket, then spin the filter on by hand until it contacts the mounting surface, then 3/4 turn more.
Reinstall the drain plug. Torque to 25 ft-lbs. Don't gorilla it — the oil pan is thin steel and the threads strip.
Add 6 quarts (4.0L) or 5 quarts (5.2/5.9L) of fresh oil. Start the engine, watch the pressure light go out within 5 seconds, then shut down.
Wait 5 minutes for the oil to settle, then check the dipstick. Top off to the full mark.
Recycle the old oil — every AutoZone and O'Reilly takes used oil free.
pros: Cheapest maintenance job on the vehicle, and the one that does the most for longevity
The Magnum V8s and the 4.0L share the same filter — one part to stock
Good filter access compared to most modern vehicles (no skid plate to drop, no fender liner to peel)
cons: The drain plug is at the lowest point of a thin steel pan — over-torque it once and you're tapping threads or replacing the pan
The oil filter dumps oil down the frame rail when you spin it off — pre-position cardboard or wipe up after
Magnums burn a little oil between changes by 150K — check the dipstick monthly, not at oil-change time

title: Spark Plugs — 4.0L and 5.2/5.9 Magnum

citations.title: Champion RC12LYC fits 4.0L and Magnum V8 ZJs
ZJ spark plug specs reference

summary: All three ZJ engines run the Champion RC12LYC (or NGK ZFR5N), gapped at 0.035". The 4.0L is a 15-minute job; the Magnum V8s take an hour because the rear plugs hide behind the exhaust manifolds.
description:
The ZJ is one of the rare vehicles where every factory engine option runs the same spark plug. Champion's RC12LYC is the OEM unit — Mopar boxes it as part number 56027275. Gap them to 0.035" before installation, even brand-new in the box; plug gaps drift in shipping and a tight gap will make the 4.0L stumble on cold mornings.

NGK ZFR5N is the equivalent if you can't find Champions. Skip the platinum and iridium upgrades — these engines were designed for copper-electrode plugs, and the high-energy plugs don't last meaningfully longer in a low-compression motor like the 4.0L. Spend the money you save on a real coil pack and cap-and-rotor kit.

On the 4.0L straight-six, all six plugs are on the passenger side of the head, fully accessible from above. Pop the wires off one at a time (don't pull all six and try to remember the firing order — pull, swap, replace, move on). On the Magnum V8s, the front three plugs on each side come out from above; the rear plugs require either a long extension and patience, or removing a wheel and going through the wheel well. Both Magnum approaches work — the wheel-well route is faster after you've done it once.

Anti-seize on the threads is mandatory on the iron heads of the 4.0L — without it, you'll pull aluminum thread material out of the head on the next change. The Magnum V8s also have iron heads; anti-seize is still recommended. Use a light coat — too much and you'll over-torque the plug because the friction is misleading.
steps: Let the engine cool fully. Pulling plugs from a warm aluminum-headed engine pulls threads; the ZJ has iron heads but the rule still applies — cold is better.
Number the spark plug wires with masking tape (1-2-3-4-5-6 on the I6, 1-3-5-7 driver side and 2-4-6-8 passenger on the V8s). This saves you if the firing order on the cap is unclear.
Working one cylinder at a time: pull the wire from the plug by gripping the boot (not the wire), then remove the plug with the 5/8" spark plug socket.
Gap the new plug to 0.035" using a wire-style gap tool. Check every plug — don't trust the factory gap.
Apply a thin coat of anti-seize to the plug threads (the threads, not the electrode).
Hand-thread the new plug into the head — if it doesn't spin in easily by hand, back it out and try again. Cross-threading the head is a $300 mistake.
Torque the plug. 4.0L: 27 ft-lbs. Magnum V8s: 30 ft-lbs.
Apply a small dab of dielectric grease to the inside of the wire boot, then reinstall the wire. You should feel and hear it click onto the plug.
Repeat for each cylinder. Start the engine and listen for a smooth idle — if it stumbles, you missed a wire.
pros: All three ZJ engines share the same plug — one set in your spares kit covers the whole platform
Champion RC12LYC is under $4 a plug — cheapest scheduled-maintenance item on the truck
Fresh plugs noticeably wake up a tired Magnum V8 and steady out the 4.0L's idle
cons: The rear plugs on the Magnum V8s are buried behind the exhaust manifolds — patience required
Iron heads are forgiving but cross-threading still happens — always hand-start every plug
Skip the platinum/iridium upgrade hype — these engines don't benefit from it

title: Transfer Case Fluid — NP242 and NP249
tools_required: 3/8" ratchet (no socket — the plug has a square drive head)
fluid pump (hand pump or squeeze bottle with hose)

citations.title: ZJ NP242/NP249 fluid capacity and procedure
NP242 fluid change reference

summary: Both the NP242 (Selec-Trac) and NP249 (Quadra-Trac) in the ZJ take ATF. The NP242 holds 1.4 quarts; the NP249 holds 1.25 quarts. Buy 2 quarts of any name-brand ATF and you've got the job covered. Plan on 30 minutes.
description:
The ZJ shipped with one of three transfer cases: the NP231 (rare, manual transmission only), the NP242 Selec-Trac (the part-time/full-time selectable case that most ZJs got), and the NP249 Quadra-Trac (full-time with a viscous coupling — found mostly on the Limited and Orvis trims). All three take ATF, not gear oil. Running gear oil in any of them will destroy the viscous coupling (NP249) or the planetary gears (NP242). Don't experiment.

ATF type doesn't matter much — the original Mopar spec was Dexron II, but ATF+4 works fine and is what's on the parts store shelf today. Valvoline MaxLife is a popular budget choice and has run trouble-free in thousands of ZJs. The NP249 with a worn viscous coupling will shudder in tight turns at low speed regardless of fluid — that's a coupling failure, not a fluid problem.

The fill and drain plugs are both 3/8" square drive — no socket needed. Stick your 3/8" ratchet directly into the plug. Crack the fill plug first, before you drain — if the fill plug is seized, you don't want to find out after you've emptied the case. Some old fill plugs round off; have a pair of vice grips on standby.
steps: Drive the vehicle for 10 minutes to warm the fluid. Warm fluid drains faster and carries out more contamination.
Park on a level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels. Raise the rear of the vehicle (you can do this with both rear wheels on jack stands, or with the whole vehicle on a lift).
Locate the transfer case behind the transmission. The fill plug is on the upper rear; the drain plug is on the lower rear.
Crack the fill plug first. If it spins out, you're clear to drain. Reinstall it loosely.
Position the drain pan under the drain plug. Remove the drain plug. Let it drain fully — usually 3–5 minutes.
Inspect the magnetic drain plug (NP242 has one, NP249 does not). A light film of metallic dust is normal; chunks or shavings mean internal damage and a fluid change won't fix it.
Wipe the drain plug clean, reinstall, torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Remove the fill plug. Pump fresh ATF into the case until fluid runs out the fill hole (not down — out, level). NP242: about 1.4 quarts. NP249: about 1.25 quarts.
Reinstall the fill plug, torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Lower the vehicle. Take it for a short drive and re-check for leaks at both plugs.
pros: Cheapest drivetrain service on the ZJ — under $20 in fluid
The magnetic drain plug on the NP242 gives you a free condition report each time you service the case
Fresh ATF restores smooth shifting between 2H/4H/4L modes on the NP242
cons: Both fill and drain plugs use a 3/8" square drive head that rounds off easily on old, dry cases — bring vice grips
NP249 shudder in tight turns at low speed is a viscous coupling failure, not fixable with new fluid — it's a transfer case rebuild or a swap to NP242
Overfilling pushes fluid out the vent and onto your exhaust — fill level is "until it runs out the fill hole," not "as much as the spec card says"

title: Track Bar Replacement and Upgrade

parts.name: Heavy-duty adjustable track bar (Core 4x4 Cruise Series)
Kevin's Offroad Hard-KOR track bar conversion

citations.title: Kevin's Offroad — Death Wobble cures and ZJ track bar conversions
Core 4x4 — ZJ Cruise Series adjustable track bar

summary: The front track bar holds the axle laterally centered under the truck. A worn track bar lets the axle dance side to side over bumps, and on a coil-sprung four-link like the ZJ that's a primary cause of death wobble. Replace the bar before chasing anything else if the steering wheel oscillates at speed.
description:
The ZJ front track bar is one of the weakest links in the steering system. The bushing at the frame end fails (sometimes you can see daylight through the bushing eye), and the threaded upper rod end develops play. Both ends contribute to lateral axle slop. Even on a perfectly aligned, stock-height ZJ, a worn track bar will produce wandering steering and feel like a soft tie rod.

Two upgrade paths. Stock-replacement bars (Moog DS1417, Mopar OE) get you back to factory tightness for under $100 — the right call for daily-driven, stock-height ZJs. Adjustable heavy-duty bars (Core 4x4 Cruise Series, Kevin's Offroad Hard-KOR) use DOM tubing, a Johnny Joint or heim at the adjustable end, and a polyurethane or solid bushing at the fixed end. They tighten the front end noticeably and recenter the axle if you've lifted the truck. Plan on $250–$300 for a real heavy-duty kit.

Frame bracket warning: the factory track bar bracket on the frame is stamped steel and bends over time, especially on lifted ZJs. If the frame end of the bar tracks visibly bent, you need a reinforced bracket (StinkyFab and Iron Rock both make them) — installing a heavy-duty track bar onto a bent factory bracket lasts about six months.

Death wobble note. The track bar is one of five components to inspect if you have death wobble. The other four: ball joints, tie rod ends, steering box (sector shaft play), and unit bearings. Replacing the track bar alone solves death wobble maybe 40% of the time. Combine it with ball joint and tie rod checks for an 80–95% cure rate. See the related ZJ death wobble guide.

Service interval: inspect at every oil change. Replace when the bushing tears or when the threaded end has visible play.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the front of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands. Both front wheels off the ground.
Remove the front wheels for working access (optional but recommended).
Soak both track bar bolts with PB Blaster. Let it work for 10 minutes.

Remove the axle-end bolt (21mm). The axle end is typically a tapered stud that needs a tie rod puller or sharp hammer blow on the bracket to break free. Don't beat directly on the stud — you'll mushroom it.
Remove the frame-end bolt (18mm). The bushing end is a straight-through bolt.
Lift the old track bar out. Compare the new bar's length on the bench to make sure you have the right part.
Install the new bar. If it's adjustable, set the length so the front axle sits centered under the truck — measure from a fixed frame point to each tire sidewall and adjust until both sides match.
Bolt the new track bar in hand-tight at both ends.
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight on the ground.

With the truck at ride height, torque both bolts to 74 ft-lbs (FSM spec for the 1993-1998 ZJ — verify in your service manual). Torquing at ride height (not at full droop) is mandatory so the bushing isn't preloaded.
Re-check axle centering by measuring frame-to-tire on both sides. If off, adjust an adjustable bar; on a stock bar, slight off-center is unavoidable and the alignment shop will compensate.
Drive 20 miles. Re-check torque on both ends.
Schedule an alignment within 200 miles — track bar replacement shifts caster slightly.
pros: Single biggest steering improvement on a tired ZJ for the dollar
One of the five core components in any death-wobble diagnosis
Adjustable bars let you recenter the axle on lifted trucks — required above 2.5" of lift
cons: A new track bar alone won't fix death wobble if the ball joints, tie rods, or steering box are also worn
Beating on the axle-end stud with a hammer damages the threads — use a tie rod puller or a careful side-blow on the bracket
Skipping the torque-at-ride-height step preloads the bushing and shortens its life
Alignment is needed after — budget another $100–$150 at a shop

title: Control Arm and Bushing Replacement
tools_required: bushing press or shop press (if reusing arms with new bushings)
rotary tool or hacksaw (cutting out stuck bushings)
skills_required: bushing pressing or replacing complete arms

parts.name: Energy Suspension polyurethane bushing kit (full set)

citations.title: Quadratec — ZJ control arm bushings catalog
JeepForum — ZJ front lower control arm bushing replacement

summary: Both ZJ axles use a four-link with rubber-bushed control arms. After 25 years the bushings are torn, sloppy, or missing chunks — they steer the truck around like a drunk pendulum. Replace complete arms instead of pressing in new bushings unless you own a shop press. The labor difference makes new arms the better deal for most owners.
description:
Three failure modes give themselves away. A clunk on takeoff after parking on a slope is a torn lower control arm bushing on the front. Wandering steering on highway at speed is upper control arm bushing play. A "click-click-click" over expansion joints in cold weather is the rear lower control arm bushing. Get under the truck with a pry bar and lever each arm at the axle end — if you can move it noticeably, the bushing is gone.

Buying decisions. Complete replacement arms with bushings pre-pressed run $50–$80 per arm in Moog or Mevotech. Pressing new bushings into your existing arms saves money but requires a shop press, a bushing driver set, and patience for the stuck ones — figure 2–3 hours per arm versus 45 minutes for a complete-arm swap. The complete arm is the better deal unless you already have the press.

Polyurethane bushings (Energy Suspension 2.3104G) last longer and tighten up the truck's handling at the cost of more noise transmission and faster wear at the ball joint end. Rubber is fine for daily drivers. Poly is the right call if you've already accepted the squeak in trade for tight steering.

Pinion angle warning: if you've lifted the ZJ above 2.5", stock-length control arms will pull the pinion up at the front and down at the rear. Adjustable arms (Iron Rock, Currie, JKS) fix this. Stock arms with stock geometry are correct on stock-height ZJs.
steps: Loosen the lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the front of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands. Both wheels off the ground.
Remove the front wheels.
Support the front axle with a floor jack so it doesn't drop when the lower arm comes free.
Soak the lower arm bolts with PB Blaster. Let it work for 15 minutes.
Remove the front lower control arm bolt at the axle end (21mm). It may need a breaker bar — the bolt sees a lot of stress.
Remove the front lower control arm bolt at the frame end (21mm).
Lift the arm out. If a bushing is stuck on a bolt sleeve, use a long pry bar to walk it off.
Install the new arm with new hardware (the kits include new bolts and nuts — use them; the old bolts are weakened from corrosion). Torque hand-tight only for now.
Repeat steps 5–8 for the front upper arm. The upper arm bolts are tighter to reach — a swivel socket on a long extension is the trick.
Repeat for the opposite side. Then move to the rear axle.
Rear lower arms (21mm at axle, 21mm at frame). Same procedure — support the axle, remove old, install new.
Rear upper arms (21mm at axle, 18mm at frame on most years).
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight on the ground.
Torque all four lower arm bolts to 100 ft-lbs. Torque all four upper arm bolts to 75 ft-lbs. (Verify in the FSM for your year — some V8 ZJs spec slightly different values.)
Drive 20 miles and re-check all torque values. Bushings settle in the first few hundred miles.
pros: Restores steering precision — a ZJ with all 8 arms fresh feels 10 years younger
Most ZJs on the road today have at least 2 arms with torn bushings — fixing them is the single biggest handling upgrade
Complete-arm replacement is straightforward DIY work with hand tools
cons: Pressing bushings into the original arms requires a shop press and a lot of patience
Polyurethane bushings squeak in cold weather — many owners regret them on daily drivers
The upper arm frame bolts are in a tight space; expect skinned knuckles
Torque at ride height is mandatory or the bushing preloads and tears early

title: Quadra-Coil Rear Suspension Service
tools_required: second floor jack or pole jack (to support axle)

parts.name: Sway bar end links (pair, if rotted)

citations.title: Cherokee Forum — ZJ/WJ coil spring replacement how-to
Quadratec — ZJ coil springs catalog

summary: ZJ Quadra-Coil rear is a four-link with coil springs — same architecture as the XJ and TJ rear, with two lower arms, two uppers, a track bar, and a coil over each spring perch. Service is straightforward once you know to support the axle before you unbolt anything.
description:
The Quadra-Coil name was Chrysler's marketing for "coil springs front and rear" — there is no air, no electronic damping, no exotic geometry. Front and rear are both solid-axle coil-sprung four-link setups. That's part of why the ZJ runs circles around the later WK on a trail: it's a genuinely capable platform with straightforward suspension. Stock coils sag after 25 years and will let the bump stops touch the axle tube on a hard compression. Stock shocks are toast on any ZJ that hasn't seen new ones in the last decade.

Decisions before you order parts. If the ZJ rides like a brick and sits low in the rear, replace coils and shocks together. If it rides okay but bottoms out over speed bumps, do shocks. Bilstein 5100 is the gold-standard street/light-trail shock for a stock-height ZJ. Rancho RS5000X is the budget pick. Monroe and KYB white-box shocks are economy options — they work but won't outlast Bilsteins.

Lift options: A 2" lift spring upgrade is the sweet spot for 31" tires. Iron Rock Off Road, Old Man Emu, and Rusty's all make ZJ-specific 2" lift coils. Anything taller than 3" on a ZJ requires adjustable control arms and a longer track bar — see the related control arm guide.

Service interval: shocks every 60,000–80,000 miles, springs only when sagging or damaged. Inspect upper coil isolators every shock change — they crumble and let the spring contact bare metal.
steps: Loosen the rear lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the rear of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands forward of the lower control arm mounts.
Remove the wheels.
Place a second floor jack under the axle differential housing, snug but not lifting.
Disconnect the rear sway bar end links (15mm). If they're rotted, replace them rather than fight to save them.
Remove the lower shock bolt (18mm) on each side. Pull the shocks free at the bottom and let them hang on the upper mount.
Disconnect the rear track bar at the axle (21mm). This lets the axle drop straight down rather than swing sideways.
Slowly lower the floor jack under the axle. The coil springs will extend and eventually unseat. Stop when the springs are loose — usually 4–6" of axle drop.
Remove the coil springs by hand. They lift right out once unloaded.
Inspect the upper coil isolators in the frame pocket. Replace if cracked or crumbling.
Set the new coil springs in the lower spring perch and align them in the upper isolator pocket. Make sure the coil end seats in the locator notch in the lower perch.
Raise the axle back up with the floor jack. The springs should compress into place as the axle rises.
Reconnect the track bar (21mm) but don't fully torque yet. Reconnect the sway bar end links.
Install new shocks: lower bolt 23 ft-lbs, upper nut 23 ft-lbs (typical — verify in service manual for your year).
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight, then torque the track bar bolt to 74 ft-lbs. Torquing at ride height (not droop) is what keeps the bushing from preloading.
Re-torque all suspension bolts to spec.
Drive 20 miles and re-check all fasteners.
pros: Restores correct ride height — a sagged ZJ rear changes pinion angle and stresses the slip yoke
New shocks transform the truck's road manners — old gas-charged ZJ shocks lose damping by 80,000 miles
A genuinely DIY-friendly Quadra-Coil rear — no spring compressors needed if you support the axle
cons: Failure to torque the track bar at ride height preloads the bushing and you'll feel it through the steering on every bump
Upper coil isolators are cheap but straightforward to forget — replace them while you're in there
Lift coils plus stock control arms = ugly pinion angle; budget for adjustable arms above 2.5"
